blocks.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

people.name: Ruth Calloway
people.role: Adviser to schools on digital learning who argues that typing skills deserve more classroom time

people.name: Annelise Moreau
people.role: Psychologist who compared handwritten and laptop note-taking among fourteen-year-olds

people.name: Daniyar Petrossian
people.role: Head of a primary school that reintroduced daily handwriting practice

paragraphs.text: Walk into almost any secondary classroom today and you are likely to see more screens than exercise books. Pupils draft essays on laptops, submit homework through online platforms and, increasingly, sit examinations on computers. Against this background, a question that would once have seemed absurd is now asked seriously by parents and policymakers alike: why should children spend hundreds of hours learning to form letters with a pen when they will spend most of their adult lives typing? It is a fair question, and it deserves a better answer than nostalgia. My own view is that handwriting should remain a core part of early education, but for reasons that have little to do with tradition.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The case against handwriting is not foolish. Ruth Calloway, who advises schools on digital learning, points out that typing is faster for most fluent users, produces text that is easy to edit and share, and removes a barrier for children whose control of a pencil develops slowly. In her experience, some pupils who struggle to write legibly become far more willing to express themselves once they are allowed a keyboard. She argues that the time spent drilling joined-up letters could be better used teaching pupils to touch-type, search for information and judge the reliability of what they find online. These are genuine skills, and any curriculum that ignores them is failing its students. Calloway is no enemy of the pen; she simply believes its place in the timetable has become too large.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Yet her argument rests on an assumption that handwriting is simply a slower way of recording words. There is growing evidence that it is also a way of learning them. Researchers have found that when young children practise forming letters by hand, they tend to recognise those letters more readily afterwards than children who learn them by pressing keys. The likely explanation is that drawing a letter forces the learner to attend to its shape, stroke by stroke, whereas a key produces an identical, finished symbol whatever the hand does. In other words, the effort that makes handwriting slow may be precisely what makes it valuable.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: A study by the psychologist Annelise Moreau points in a similar direction for older pupils. She asked two groups of fourteen-year-olds to take notes during a short lecture, one group writing by hand and the other using laptops. When tested a week later, the two groups remembered roughly the same number of facts, but the handwriting group performed noticeably better on questions that required them to explain ideas in their own words. Moreau suggests that because people writing by hand cannot keep pace with a speaker, they are obliged to summarise, and summarising requires them to process meaning rather than merely transcribe sound. She is careful to describe her results as preliminary, and her sample was small. Nonetheless, the study fits a pattern that many teachers have long observed informally.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: One such teacher is Daniyar Petrossian, head of a primary school that reintroduced daily handwriting practice after several years of relying mainly on tablets. He had noticed, he says, that pupils' spelling was growing weaker, partly because automatic correction software fixed their errors before the children were even aware of them. After the change, spelling scores rose steadily over two years, although Petrossian admits that the school also hired an extra reading specialist during the same period, so he cannot be sure which change mattered more. His frankness is welcome. Debates about education are too often settled by anecdote presented as proof, and claims for handwriting deserve the same scrutiny as claims for any new technology.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: None of this means schools should return to the classrooms of a century ago, where children were punished for untidy loops and every pupil was expected to produce the same elegant script. That approach confused handwriting with penmanship, treating appearance as the goal rather than fluency. What matters is that a child can write quickly and legibly enough that the physical act no longer absorbs their attention, leaving the mind free to concentrate on ideas. Once that point is reached, the decorative extras of traditional cursive add little, and the time saved can reasonably be given to typing.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: There is also a practical argument that is rarely heard. Technology fails: batteries run flat, networks go down, and examinations in many subjects still require written answers. Teachers who have supervised a room of pupils whose laptops have suddenly lost power will know how quickly a lesson can collapse. A pupil who has never developed a comfortable, reasonably fast hand is at a disadvantage in all of these situations, through no fault of their own.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The real choice, then, is not between pen and keyboard but about sequence and balance. Children should learn to write by hand first, because it appears to support the early recognition of letters and words, and they should learn to type well later, because the adult world demands it. Treating the two as rivals has produced a debate that generates more heat than light. Treating them as partners would give children the best of both, and that, rather than a nostalgic defence of the fountain pen, is the case worth making.
paragraphs.label: H

section.text:
Why the Pencil Still Matters

A. Walk into almost any secondary classroom today and you are likely to see more screens than exercise books. Pupils draft essays on laptops, submit homework through online platforms and, increasingly, sit examinations on computers. Against this background, a question that would once have seemed absurd is now asked seriously by parents and policymakers alike: why should children spend hundreds of hours learning to form letters with a pen when they will spend most of their adult lives typing? It is a fair question, and it deserves a better answer than nostalgia. My own view is that handwriting should remain a core part of early education, but for reasons that have little to do with tradition.

B. The case against handwriting is not foolish. Ruth Calloway, who advises schools on digital learning, points out that typing is faster for most fluent users, produces text that is easy to edit and share, and removes a barrier for children whose control of a pencil develops slowly. In her experience, some pupils who struggle to write legibly become far more willing to express themselves once they are allowed a keyboard. She argues that the time spent drilling joined-up letters could be better used teaching pupils to touch-type, search for information and judge the reliability of what they find online. These are genuine skills, and any curriculum that ignores them is failing its students. Calloway is no enemy of the pen; she simply believes its place in the timetable has become too large.

C. Yet her argument rests on an assumption that handwriting is simply a slower way of recording words. There is growing evidence that it is also a way of learning them. Researchers have found that when young children practise forming letters by hand, they tend to recognise those letters more readily afterwards than children who learn them by pressing keys. The likely explanation is that drawing a letter forces the learner to attend to its shape, stroke by stroke, whereas a key produces an identical, finished symbol whatever the hand does. In other words, the effort that makes handwriting slow may be precisely what makes it valuable.

D. A study by the psychologist Annelise Moreau points in a similar direction for older pupils. She asked two groups of fourteen-year-olds to take notes during a short lecture, one group writing by hand and the other using laptops. When tested a week later, the two groups remembered roughly the same number of facts, but the handwriting group performed noticeably better on questions that required them to explain ideas in their own words. Moreau suggests that because people writing by hand cannot keep pace with a speaker, they are obliged to summarise, and summarising requires them to process meaning rather than merely transcribe sound. She is careful to describe her results as preliminary, and her sample was small. Nonetheless, the study fits a pattern that many teachers have long observed informally.

E. One such teacher is Daniyar Petrossian, head of a primary school that reintroduced daily handwriting practice after several years of relying mainly on tablets. He had noticed, he says, that pupils' spelling was growing weaker, partly because automatic correction software fixed their errors before the children were even aware of them. After the change, spelling scores rose steadily over two years, although Petrossian admits that the school also hired an extra reading specialist during the same period, so he cannot be sure which change mattered more. His frankness is welcome. Debates about education are too often settled by anecdote presented as proof, and claims for handwriting deserve the same scrutiny as claims for any new technology.

F. None of this means schools should return to the classrooms of a century ago, where children were punished for untidy loops and every pupil was expected to produce the same elegant script. That approach confused handwriting with penmanship, treating appearance as the goal rather than fluency. What matters is that a child can write quickly and legibly enough that the physical act no longer absorbs their attention, leaving the mind free to concentrate on ideas. Once that point is reached, the decorative extras of traditional cursive add little, and the time saved can reasonably be given to typing.

G. There is also a practical argument that is rarely heard. Technology fails: batteries run flat, networks go down, and examinations in many subjects still require written answers. Teachers who have supervised a room of pupils whose laptops have suddenly lost power will know how quickly a lesson can collapse. A pupil who has never developed a comfortable, reasonably fast hand is at a disadvantage in all of these situations, through no fault of their own.

H. The real choice, then, is not between pen and keyboard but about sequence and balance. Children should learn to write by hand first, because it appears to support the early recognition of letters and words, and they should learn to type well later, because the adult world demands it. Treating the two as rivals has produced a debate that generates more heat than light. Treating them as partners would give children the best of both, and that, rather than a nostalgic defence of the fountain pen, is the case worth making.

explanation.ru: В абзаце B говорится, что, по мнению Calloway, время, которое уходит на «drilling joined-up letters», лучше было бы потратить на обучение печати («typing») и другим цифровым навыкам («digital skills»).
explanation.uk: В абзаці B сказано, що, на думку Calloway, час, який іде на «drilling joined-up letters», краще було б витратити на навчання друку («typing») та інших цифрових навичок («digital skills»).

questions.prompt: Whatever movement the hand makes, pressing a key results in the same ______.
questions.evidence: a key produces an identical, finished symbol whatever the hand does

explanation.en: Paragraph C explains that a key always produces an identical, finished symbol, unlike drawing a letter stroke by stroke.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C объясняется, что клавиша всегда даёт одинаковый («identical») готовый символ, в отличие от буквы, которую рисуют штрих за штрихом.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C пояснюється, що клавіша завжди дає однаковий («identical») готовий символ, на відміну від літери, яку малюють штрих за штрихом.

questions.prompt: Moreau acknowledges that her sample was small and calls her results ______.
questions.evidence: She is careful to describe her results as preliminary, and her sample was small.

explanation.en: Paragraph D says Moreau carefully describes her results as preliminary, meaning early and not yet certain.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D говорится, что Moreau осторожно называет свои результаты предварительными («preliminary»), то есть ранними и пока не окончательными.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D сказано, що Moreau обережно називає свої результати попередніми («preliminary»), тобто ранніми й ще не остаточними.

questions.prompt: Before reintroducing daily handwriting practice, Petrossian's school had depended largely on ______.
questions.evidence: after several years of relying mainly on tablets

explanation.en: Paragraph E says the school had relied mainly on tablets for several years before bringing back handwriting practice.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E говорится, что несколько лет школа в основном полагалась на планшеты («tablets»), прежде чем вернуть занятия письмом от руки.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E сказано, що кілька років школа здебільшого покладалася на планшети («tablets»), перш ніж повернути заняття з письма від руки.
